verdict.rationale: The lexical pattern across Gen 1:26-27, Gen 2:7, and Gen 2:21-22 names God as the direct and personal agent of humanity's origin, and the witness reaches the New Testament. Four verbs carry the load: bara (H1254A, queried across all 39 verses with God as the only subject) creates the human and is repeated three times in Gen 1:27 with the human as eth-marked direct object; yatsar (H3335, the potter verb) forms the man from dust; naphach (H5301) blows the breath of life into his nostrils; banah (H1129) builds the woman from his side. Matt 19:4 (ktizo, poieo) and 1 Tim 2:13 (plasso, the Greek mirror of yatsar) restate Adam and the man-female pair as a divine making, so the spread is pan-canonical. The reading that the words affirm divine agency without specifying biological mechanism is also lexically defensible, since yatsar is used of God forming individuals in the womb (Jer 1:5, Isa 44:2, Ps 139:16), which is a real mediate process. The affirmed point (direct divine agency) is decisive; the question of mechanism is what the vocabulary underdetermines.

scripture.force: The clause naaseh adam (let us make man) uses a deliberate first-person volitive of asah, which sets the human-making apart from the impersonal jussives that produce the prior days. The pair tselem and demuth assigns the human a categorial likeness to God that no other created thing receives. The verb here names intention and personal resolve, not a process. It tells who acts and with what purpose, but it does not by itself specify the physical manner of execution.

Bara occurs three times in this single verse with Elohim as subject and the human as direct object marked by the accusative particle eth. A direct query of all 39 verses where bara (H1254A) appears confirms that it never takes a human or natural subject in the canon, it is reserved for divine action. Male and female (zakar, neqebah) are both named at the originating creation event, not introduced as a later branch. The grammar fixes God as the agent. It does not in this verse describe the bodily steps of the making.

Wayyitser (yatsar) is the potter verb. God forms the man of dust (aphar) from the ground, then blows (naphach) the neshamah of life into his nostrils, and only at that point does the man become a living nephesh. The clause order makes the divine breath the proximate cause of human animation. A full concordance pull of yatsar (54 distinct verses) shows the same verb used of God forming the prophet in the womb (Jer 1:5) and forming Israel from the womb (Isa 44:2, Isa 44:24, Isa 49:5), processes that unfold through ordinary gestation, so yatsar names personal divine craftsmanship without fixing whether the forming is immediate or works through a means.

Tardemah is a divinely induced deep sleep, the same noun used in Gen 15:12 of the covenant theophany with Abram (confirmed by query, 7 occurrences total). God takes a tsela (side or rib) from the man and closes (sagar) flesh in its place. The verbs narrate a concrete, intentional, hands-on act rather than a figurative cause or a gradual emergence.

Banah, the verb for building or constructing (340 occurrences, normally of houses, cities, and altars), governs the formation of the woman from the side material taken from the man. The grammar makes the woman a derived but discrete act of divine construction with God as the named builder, not a parallel line that arose on its own.

The same verb wayyitser (yatsar) used of the man in Gen 2:7 is also used here of the land animals and birds, formed by God from the ground. This shows that the forming verb alone is not what marks the human as special. What is not repeated for any animal is the breathing of God's own neshamah and the threefold bara of Gen 1:27. This text complicates a naive reading that leans only on yatsar, and it also constrains the evolutionary reading, because the animals too are said to be formed directly by God from the ground.

The land animals are produced by a mediated formula, totse haarets (let the earth bring forth) using the causative of yatsa. This is a different construction from the human-making, which uses bara plus eth-adam and the personal naaseh. The contrast within Gen 1 itself, mediated bringing-forth for the animals versus direct creation language for the human, sharpens rather than weakens the directness claimed for the human.

The judgment oracle confirms the Gen 2:7 origin by returning the man to the dust he was taken from, ki aphar attah (for you are dust). The aphar idiom is treated as a real statement of where the man came from, not as poetic dress, and it assumes the original forming as an actual event.

The toledoth header of adam restates that on the day God created adam he made him in the demuth of God. The genealogical header treats Gen 1 and Gen 2 as a single historical origin point for the human line, with God as maker.

Before I formed you (yatsar) in the womb I knew you. Here the identical potter verb describes God forming an individual person through ordinary gestation in the womb (ba-beten). This is the strongest lexical basis for the reading that yatsar affirms personal divine forming without by itself excluding a mediate biological means. It does not overturn the directness in Genesis, but it shows the verb does not settle the question of mechanism.

The LORD your maker (osekha) and your former (yotserkha) from the womb (mi-beten). The same verb pair, asah and yatsar, that operates in the Genesis human-making is here applied to God forming a person from the womb. This is part of the lexical evidence that the forming vocabulary asserts divine agency over a person's origin while remaining compatible with a process that runs in time.

My days were formed (yatsar, passive) when as yet there were none. The verb of Gen 2:7 is used of the shaping of a life across time. This further shows that yatsar names God's purposeful forming of a person without specifying an instantaneous manner, which is the genuine point the Genesis vocabulary leaves open.

Job locates his own continuing life in the neshamah in his nostrils and the ruach of Eloah, recycling the exact Gen 2:7 vocabulary. The wisdom text treats the Gen 2:7 breath as the ongoing description of every living human, which presses the originating divine breath as a real cause and not a figure.

The flood narrative uses neshamath ruach chayyim (the breath of the spirit of life) in the nostrils to describe what dies, presupposing the Gen 2:7 source of that breath as the common origin of human and creaturely life.

Isaiah stacks all three Genesis verbs on the same human object, beratiw (I created him), yetsartiw (I formed him), aph asitiw (indeed I made him). The triple chain gathers the Gen 1 and Gen 2 vocabulary together and insists that God is the agent of the human's existence. The piling of synonyms intensifies the agency claim without itemizing the physical steps.

He made us (asanu) and not we ourselves. The negation places the cause of human existence outside human agency and assigns it to God as maker. It directly excludes a self-originating account, which is the contrast the proposition's negation targets.

Jesus says the one who created (ho ktisas) from the beginning made them (epoiesen autous) male and female (arsen kai thelu), directly echoing the zakar and neqebah of Gen 1:27. This carries the same agent-and-act grammar into the New Testament and attributes the male and female pairing to a personal creator at the beginning, which gives the doctrine an OT and NT spread.

Adam was first formed (protos eplasthe, from plasso), then Eve. Plasso is the standard Greek mold-or-shape verb and the regular Septuagint rendering of yatsar. Applying eplasthe to Adam restates the Gen 2:7 potter-forming in Greek and ties the New Testament directly to the Genesis vocabulary, with God as the implied forming agent.

complicating_texts.resolution: The animals are also formed (yatsar) by God from the ground, so the forming verb alone does not single out the human. The distinguishing features are the threefold bara of Gen 1:27, the eth-marked direct object, the image-and-likeness assignment, and God breathing his own neshamah into the man, none of which is repeated for any animal. The human special-creation reading therefore rests on the cluster, not on yatsar by itself.

Yatsar is used of God forming an individual in the womb (ba-beten), a process that runs through ordinary gestation, and the same womb-forming use appears in Isa 44:2, Isa 44:24, Isa 49:5, and Ps 139:16. This shows the verb predicates personal divine agency over a person's origin but does not by itself fix whether the forming is instantaneous or works through a means. The proposition's affirmed core (direct divine agency) holds; the additional claim about excluding any mediate process is what the vocabulary leaves open. This is recorded as a genuine, fairly stated competing lens rather than a defeater.

Land animals are produced by the mediated totse haarets formula (let the earth bring forth), which is grammatically distinct from the direct bara plus naaseh language used of the human. The contrast supports the directness claimed for the human-making and does not undercut it.

variants.note: The anchor verses are in Genesis, outside the ingested ECM window (3 John). Gen 1 and Gen 2 sit in the Masoretic and Samaritan Pentateuch consonantal stream with no variant readings that touch the bara, yatsar, naphach, neshamah, tsela, or banah anchors. The New Testament witnesses cited (Matt 19:4 ktizo and poieo, 1 Tim 2:13 plasso) have no variant that changes which creation verb is used. CBGM is not applicable to these verses.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the verb cluster (bara three times, the personal naaseh, yatsar from dust, naphach of the breath, banah of the woman from the rib) as discrete, hands-on divine acts that produced the first human pair immediately, with the contrast against the mediated totse haarets of the animals and the unique image-and-likeness assignment confirming that the human origin is told as a direct creative event rather than the terminus of a natural sequence.

Agrees that the words make God the personal agent of humanity's origin, but holds that the same verbs do not by themselves specify the physical manner. The strongest lexical support is that yatsar, the Gen 2:7 verb, is used of God forming individuals in the womb (Jer 1:5, Isa 44:2, Isa 44:24, Isa 49:5, Ps 139:16), a process that unfolds through ordinary gestation, and that aphar (dust) and naphach (blow, breathe) are common-language terms whose Gen 2:7 sense comes from context. On this reading the text decisively affirms that humanity is God's deliberate work and not self-originating, while leaving the biological mechanism unaddressed by the vocabulary itself. This lens still rejects an unguided, agentless account, because Ps 100:3 (he made us, not we ourselves) and the eth-marked bara of Gen 1:27 keep God as the cause.

hermeneutics.notes: The proposition has two parts: a positive claim (specially created by God) and a negation (not the product of unguided processes). Both competing lenses affirm the positive divine-agency claim and both reject an unguided, self-originating account, so the verdict affirms on the part the lexis decides. The lenses differ only on whether the vocabulary also forecloses any mediate process, which is the point the words underdetermine. Chronology frameworks (young earth, old earth, framework) do not change the agency reading and are listed as frameworks_in_play but are not the axis of divergence.

stem_audit.notes: The stem pairs a positive claim (Adam and Eve specially created by God) with a negation (not the product of unguided evolutionary processes). The negation names the actual contrast the lexis resolves, namely whether the verbs identify a deliberate divine agent or an agentless natural process, so it does not smuggle the verdict. The lexical pattern decides the agency question on its own terms. No rephrasing was needed. Affirms is unchanged from the prior file (still true); the enrichment deepened the underdetermination analysis and added the New Testament witnesses, it did not flip the verdict.

lay_summary: Genesis tells the origin of Adam and Eve with a cluster of verbs that name God as the personal agent. Bara, the creation verb the Hebrew Bible reserves for God (a query of all its occurrences finds no human or natural subject), appears three times in Gen 1:27 with the human as the direct object. Before that, Gen 1:26 uses a deliberate let us make, not the impersonal commands of earlier days, and assigns the human the image and likeness of God, which nothing else receives. Yatsar, the potter verb, shapes the man from dust in Gen 2:7, and God blows the breath of life into his nostrils, at which point the man becomes a living being. Banah, the building verb, makes the woman from the man's side. Ps 100:3 adds the plain negation, he made us and not we ourselves, and the New Testament keeps the same grammar: Jesus says the creator made them male and female (Matt 19:4) and Paul says Adam was first formed, using the Greek verb that translates the Hebrew potter verb (1 Tim 2:13). So the words decisively say humanity is God's deliberate work, not a self-originating accident. Why do careful readers still divide? The divergence is lexical, not historical. The very verb used of forming the man, yatsar, is also used of God forming a person in the womb (Jer 1:5, Isa 44:2, Ps 139:16), and that forming clearly runs through an ordinary process over time. The same word, dust, and the verb to breathe are common terms whose strong creation sense here comes from context. So the vocabulary settles who acts and that the act is deliberate and personal, but it does not by itself state the physical manner, whether the forming was instantaneous or worked through a means. One reading takes the verbs as immediate, hands-on acts. The other reads them as affirming divine agency while leaving the mechanism open. Both reject an unguided, agentless origin, which is the heart of what the proposition claims, and that is why the verdict affirms.
